problem: The chapter says charging 'starts at constant current, then switches to constant voltage to avoid overcharge' without saying which chemistry. That is the lead-acid (CC then CV/float) method. Nickel-cadmium aircraft batteries are charged at constant current only, with voltage and temperature cut-offs. A constant-voltage finish on NiCd is exactly what the chapter itself says drives thermal runaway in Section 2, so a student gets two contradicting rules.
fix: Split the statement by chemistry: 'Lead-acid charges at constant current and then at constant voltage (float) to avoid overcharge. Nickel-cadmium is charged at constant current, with the charger stopped by voltage or temperature cut-off; never leave a NiCd on a constant-voltage charge, because its cell voltage falls as it heats and the current then keeps rising.'

problem: 'The battery is the only source with the engines off' reads as an absolute rule. With the engines off an APU generator or a ground power unit can be feeding the DC buses, and the battery is then a standby source, not the only one.
fix: Write 'With all generators offline, the battery is the only source, and it carries essential loads until another source comes online.'

problem: The lead-acid curve starts at 25.5 V (2.13 V per cell) and is still at 24.6 V at 40% while discharging at 1C. Those values are close to open-circuit or surface-charge values; under a steady 1C load a 12-cell battery settles near 24 V (about 2.0 V per cell) within the first minutes, then falls to the 21.4 V end point.
fix: Start the lead-acid curve near 25.2 V at 0% and let it settle quickly, for example 24.4 V at 20%, 24.0 V at 40%, 23.6 V at 60%, 23.0 V at 80% and 21.4 V at 100%, so the plotted values match a real 1C discharge.
